passage: Ganga had wanted to teach in her hometown school since she was twelve, and for two years it felt like a dream. Now the mornings tasted like chalk dust. She marked the same copies, filled the same registers, and felt nothing. "Maybe I chose wrong," she told Farhan, the head teacher, over tea at the school gate. "Which part still makes you feel something?" he asked. She thought. "The reading circle. When a child finally gets a word." "And what are you avoiding?" "The staff meetings. And the endless forms." They looked at the timetable together. By the next month Ganga ran the library corner two afternoons a week, and Farhan had taken the forms off her desk. She still had bad days. But she no longer wanted to leave everything.

qa.q: Which part of teaching still made Ganga feel something?
qa.a: The reading circle, when a child finally gets a word.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling about her career when she spoke at the school gate?
qa.a: She felt empty and doubted her choice, as shown by "Maybe I chose wrong" after two years of a dream.

qa.q: What changed in Ganga's routine, and why is that a sensible kind of change?
qa.a: She got the library corner and lost the forms. Adjusting a role and rhythm addressed what she avoided without abandoning everything.

qa.q: How does Farhan approach Ganga's doubts?
qa.a: He asks what still matters and what she avoids, then adjusts the timetable, rather than telling her to leave or to just cope.

grounding: Dream career feels empty after novelty ends; asking what still matters and what is avoided, and changing a role or rhythm rather than everything.

passage:
First week of March. Yash had wanted to be an architect since he was nine. Two years into his job at a Mumbai firm, he sat at his desk redrawing the same bathroom fittings for a tower project and felt nothing. On the local train home he wondered if he'd wasted his life.

A week later. He took his senior, Aparna, for chai. "I think I hate architecture."

"Do you?" she asked. "Or do you hate bathroom fittings?"

He laughed, then thought. "I love site visits. Talking to the workers. Figuring out how light moves in a room. I hate spreadsheets and endless revisions for a client I've never met."

"So what are you avoiding?"

"Asking for different work. In case they say no."

End of April. Yash asked. He moved to the small housing team that did site work twice a week. On Friday he stood in a half-built school classroom, watching the afternoon light fall exactly where he'd planned it.

qa.q: Since what age had Yash wanted to be an architect?
What was Yash feeling as he redrew the bathroom fittings?
qa.a: He felt empty and disillusioned, wondering if he'd wasted his life on the wrong career.

qa.q: What helped Yash see what needed to change?
qa.a: Aparna's questions helped him separate the parts he loved from the parts he hated, notice what he was avoiding, and ask to move to a different team.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Yash's frustration?
qa.a: Aparna sees it as a problem with his current tasks rather than with architecture, and helps him figure that out.

grounding: Over several weeks, the passage shows someone whose dream career feels empty, asking what still matters and what he avoids, and changing his role rather than everything.

passage:
"Farida, you're thinking of quitting teaching altogether. Before you do, listen to me.

When I, Nirmala, was twenty-five, I'd been teaching three years at a girls' school in Lucknow. I'd wanted it all my life. And suddenly it felt like a factory. Same lessons, same copies, same staff-room complaints. I dreaded Mondays.

I nearly left to join my uncle's shop.

My old headmistress sat me down. She asked me three questions. What part of the day still makes you forget the time? What are you avoiding? What do you actually want?

The first was easy: the library period, when the girls argued about stories. The second was harder: I'd stopped trying new things because I was scared of looking foolish. The third took a month.

I didn't quit. I asked to run the library and the debate club. Forty more years I taught, beta. The work didn't change much. I did."

qa.q: What part of the school day still made Nirmala forget the time?
qa.a: The library period, when the girls argued about stories.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling about teaching at twenty-five?
qa.a: She felt empty and trapped, as if school had become a factory, dreading Mondays.

qa.q: Which choice in Nirmala's story turned things around?
qa.a: Answering the headmistress's three questions and asking to run the library and debate club, changing her role instead of leaving teaching.

qa.q: How might the headmistress have seen young Nirmala's plan to quit?
qa.a: The headmistress may have sensed Nirmala still loved parts of the work and wanted her to look closer before leaving.

grounding: An elder recalls a dream career that felt empty after the novelty wore off, asking what still mattered and what she avoided, and changing her role rather than everything.
